explanation.title: Spanish Agreement & Concordance: Making Words Match

sections.subtitle: Gender Agreement: Masculine & Feminine
sections.content: GENDER AGREEMENT: Spanish nouns have gender (masculine or feminine), and articles, adjectives, and pronouns must agree. ARTICLES agree with noun gender: EL (masculine), LA (feminine). 'El libro' (the book - masculine), 'La mesa' (the table - feminine). UN (a - masculine), UNA (a - feminine). 'Un gato' (a cat - masculine), 'Una casa' (a house - feminine). ADJECTIVES agree with noun gender: Masculine adjectives often end in -o, feminine in -a. 'El libro rojo' (the red book - rojo masculine), 'La casa roja' (the red house - roja feminine). Adjectives ending in -e or consonants often stay the same: 'El coche grande, La casa grande' (both use grande). Some adjectives drop -o and add -a: 'bueno/buena, nuevo/nueva, pequeño/pequeña'. Adjectives ending in -or add -a for feminine: 'trabajador/trabajadora' (hardworking). Nationality adjectives: 'español/española, francés/francesa, alemán/alemana'. PRONOUNS agree: 'Él es alto' (He is tall - masculine), 'Ella es alta' (She is tall - feminine). Even inanimate objects have gender: 'El libro es interesante' (The book - masculine - is interesting), 'La película es interesante' (The movie - feminine - is interesting).

sections.subtitle: Number Agreement: Singular & Plural
sections.content: NUMBER AGREEMENT: Articles, adjectives, and verbs must agree with noun number (singular or plural). ARTICLES: EL/LA (singular) → LOS/LAS (plural). 'El libro' → 'Los libros', 'La casa' → 'Las casas'. UN/UNA (singular) → UNOS/UNAS (plural, meaning 'some'). 'Un gato' → 'Unos gatos', 'Una mesa' → 'Unas mesas'. ADJECTIVES: Add -s if ending in vowel, -es if ending in consonant. 'Libro rojo' → 'Libros rojos', 'Casa grande' → 'Casas grandes', 'Chico joven' → 'Chicos jóvenes' (young boy → young boys). VERBS agree with subject: 'El niño come' (The boy eats - singular), 'Los niños comen' (The boys eat - plural). Mixed gender groups use masculine plural: 'Juan y María son altos' (Juan and María are tall - altos masculine plural even though María is feminine). DEMONSTRATIVES agree: 'Este libro' (this book - masculine singular), 'Estos libros' (these books - masculine plural), 'Esta casa' (this house - feminine singular), 'Estas casas' (these houses - feminine plural). POSSESSIVES agree: 'Mi libro/Mis libros' (my book/books), 'Nuestro amigo/Nuestros amigos' (our friend/friends - masculine), 'Nuestra amiga/Nuestras amigas' (our friend/friends - feminine).

sections.subtitle: Agreement in Compound Tenses with HABER
sections.content: COMPOUND TENSES with HABER: When using haber (have) + past participle for perfect tenses, the past participle is INVARIABLE - it doesn't change for gender or number. Present perfect: 'He comido' (I have eaten - masculine speaker), 'Ella ha comido' (She has eaten - same form), 'Hemos comido' (We have eaten - same form). The participle 'comido' never changes. 'María ha estudiado' (María has studied), 'Los estudiantes han estudiado' (The students have studied - same 'estudiado'). Pluperfect: 'Había terminado' (I/he/she had finished - same form for all). 'Las chicas habían terminado' (The girls had finished - same 'terminado', no change for feminine plural). Future perfect: 'Habré llegado' (I will have arrived - same for everyone). This is different from English and other Romance languages. The rule: HABER + past participle = NO AGREEMENT. Only HABER conjugates; participle stays in -o form (technically masculine singular, but used for all). Exception: passive voice with SER changes participle, but that's not a compound tense with haber. Compare: 'He visto la película' (I have seen the movie - haber + participle, no agreement) vs 'La película fue vista' (The movie was seen - ser + participle, agrees with película).

sections.subtitle: Agreement with SER, ESTAR, and Passive Voice
sections.content: AGREEMENT with SER and ESTAR + adjectives/participles: The predicate adjective or participle must agree with the subject in gender and number. SER + adjective: 'Juan es alto' (Juan is tall - masculine), 'María es alta' (María is tall - feminine), 'Los niños son altos' (The boys are tall - masculine plural), 'Las niñas son altas' (The girls are tall - feminine plural). ESTAR + adjective: 'La puerta está abierta' (The door is open - feminine), 'Los libros están cerrados' (The books are closed - masculine plural). ESTAR + participle (resultant state): 'La carta está escrita' (The letter is written - feminine), 'Los documentos están firmados' (The documents are signed - masculine plural). The participle agrees because it functions as an adjective. PASSIVE VOICE with SER: The past participle acts as adjective and must agree. 'El libro fue escrito por Cervantes' (The book was written by Cervantes - escrito masculine singular agrees with libro). 'Las cartas fueron escritas por mi madre' (The letters were written by my mother - escritas feminine plural agrees with cartas). Remember: With HABER (have) = no agreement. With SER/ESTAR = full agreement. 'He escrito la carta' (I have written the letter - no agreement with carta) vs 'La carta está escrita' (The letter is written - escrita agrees with carta).

sections.subtitle: Agreement with Collective Nouns
sections.content: COLLECTIVE NOUNS refer to groups but are grammatically singular. Common collective nouns: GENTE (people), FAMILIA (family), EQUIPO (team), GRUPO (group), PAREJA (couple), MULTITUD (crowd), PÚBLICO (audience). VERB AGREEMENT: Collective nouns take singular verbs, even though they refer to multiple people. 'La gente está contenta' (People ARE happy - gente is singular, so está not están). 'Mi familia vive en Madrid' (My family lives in Madrid - vive singular). 'El equipo ganó el partido' (The team won the match - ganó singular). ADJECTIVE AGREEMENT: Adjectives agree with the grammatical gender/number of the collective noun, not the individuals. 'La gente es simpática' (People are nice - simpática feminine singular agrees with gente, not with the individual people). 'El público estuvo silencioso' (The audience was silent - silencioso masculine singular agrees with público). EXCEPTION: Sometimes in informal speech, speakers use plural agreement if emphasizing individuals: 'La gente estaban contentos' (less formal, emphasizing individual people). However, standard grammar requires singular: 'La gente estaba contenta'. With pronouns referring back: 'La familia llegó y ellos comieron' (The family arrived and they ate - ellos can refer to family members as individuals in the second clause).

sections.subtitle: Agreement in Complex Sentences
sections.content: RELATIVE CLAUSES: Verbs and adjectives agree with the antecedent (the noun the relative pronoun refers to). 'La chica que vive aquí es simpática' (The girl who lives here is nice - vive agrees with chica singular). 'Los chicos que estudian mucho son inteligentes' (The boys who study a lot are intelligent - estudian agrees with chicos plural). 'Busco personas que sean honestas' (I'm looking for people who are honest - sean plural agrees with personas, honestas plural adjective). COORDINATION (multiple subjects): When coordinating subjects with Y (and), the verb is plural. 'Juan y María comen pizza' (Juan and María eat pizza - comen plural). If genders are mixed, adjectives are masculine plural: 'Juan y María son altos' (altos masculine plural, default for mixed). PARTICIPIAL clauses: Past participle agrees when it modifies a noun directly. 'Compré manzanas cultivadas localmente' (I bought apples grown locally - cultivadas feminine plural agrees with manzanas). ABSOLUTE constructions: 'Terminada la reunión, nos fuimos' (The meeting finished, we left - terminada agrees with reunión feminine). QUANTIFIERS: Agreement depends on structure. 'Mucha gente vino' (Many people came - mucha agrees with gente feminine singular, vino singular verb). 'Muchas personas vinieron' (Many people came - muchas and vinieron plural). 'La mayoría de estudiantes estudia' or 'estudian' (Most students study - can be singular or plural, both accepted).

questions.question: 'El libro roj___' - Complete with the correct ending.

answers.text: rojo (masculine singular to agree with libro)

questions.hint: Libro is masculine singular, so adjective must be masculine singular: rojo.

questions.question: 'La casa roj___' - Complete with the correct ending.

answers.text: roja (feminine singular to agree with casa)

questions.hint: Casa is feminine singular, so adjective must be feminine singular: roja.

questions.question: 'El chico español, La chica ___' - What's the feminine form?
questions.hint: Nationality adjectives: español (masculine) → española (feminine).

questions.question: 'El profesor trabajador, La profesora ___' - Complete.
questions.hint: Adjectives ending in -or add -a for feminine: trabajador → trabajadora.

questions.question: 'El coche grande, La casa ___' - What form does grande take?
questions.hint: Adjectives ending in -e usually stay the same for both genders: grande.

questions.question: 'Los libros roj___' - Complete for plural.
questions.hint: Libros is masculine plural, so adjective must be masculine plural: rojos.

questions.question: 'Las casas roj___' - Complete for plural.
questions.hint: Casas is feminine plural, so adjective must be feminine plural: rojas.

questions.question: 'Juan y María son ___' (altos/altas) - Which is correct for mixed group?

answers.text: altos (masculine plural for mixed gender groups)

questions.hint: Mixed gender groups use masculine plural: altos (default for groups with both genders).

questions.question: 'He comido' (I have eaten - female speaker) - Should 'comido' change?

answers.text: No - with HABER, past participle never changes
Yes - should be 'comida' for female speaker

questions.hint: HABER + participle = NO AGREEMENT. Past participle is invariable: He comido (all genders/numbers).

questions.question: 'Las chicas han estudiado' - Should 'estudiado' change to 'estudiadas'?

answers.text: No - with HABER, participle stays invariable
Only if using SER instead of HABER

questions.hint: With HABER (han), past participle never changes: han estudiado (same for all).

questions.question: 'María ha visto la película' - Does 'visto' agree with María or película?

answers.text: Neither - with HABER, past participle doesn't agree

questions.hint: HABER = no agreement. 'Visto' stays the same regardless of subject or object.

questions.question: 'Las niñas son alt___' - Complete.
questions.hint: With SER, adjectives agree. Niñas is feminine plural, so altas.

questions.question: 'La puerta está abiert___' - Complete.
questions.hint: With ESTAR, participles/adjectives agree. Puerta is feminine singular: abierta.

questions.question: 'Los documentos están firmad___' - Complete.
questions.hint: With ESTAR, participle agrees. Documentos is masculine plural: firmados.

questions.question: 'Las cartas fueron escrit___ por mi madre' - Complete passive voice.
questions.hint: Passive voice with SER: participle agrees. Cartas is feminine plural: escritas.

questions.question: 'La gente está content___' - Complete. (gente = people)
questions.hint: GENTE (people) is grammatically feminine singular, even though it refers to multiple people: contenta.

questions.question: 'Mi familia vive/viven en Madrid' - Which verb is correct?
questions.hint: Collective nouns like FAMILIA take singular verbs: familia vive (singular).

questions.question: 'El equipo ganó/ganaron el partido' - Which is standard Spanish?
questions.hint: Collective nouns like EQUIPO take singular verbs in standard Spanish: equipo ganó.

questions.question: 'La chica que vive/viven aquí' - Which verb is correct?
questions.hint: In relative clauses, verb agrees with antecedent. Chica (singular) → vive (singular).

questions.question: 'Los chicos que estudia/estudian mucho' - Which verb is correct?
questions.hint: Relative clause verb agrees with antecedent. Chicos (plural) → estudian (plural).

questions.question: 'Juan y María come/comen pizza' - Which is correct?

answers.text: comen (plural - coordinated subjects take plural verb)

questions.hint: Coordinated subjects with Y (and) take plural verbs: Juan y María comen.

questions.question: 'Compré manzanas cultivad___ localmente' - Complete participle.
questions.hint: When participle modifies noun directly, it agrees. Manzanas (feminine plural): cultivadas.

questions.question: 'Terminada la reunión' vs 'Terminado la reunión' - Which is correct?
questions.hint: Absolute construction: participle agrees with noun. Reunión is feminine: Terminada.

questions.question: 'He escrito la carta' vs 'La carta está escrita' - Why different agreement?

answers.text: HABER = no agreement; ESTAR = agreement with subject

questions.hint: HABER + participle = invariable (escrito). ESTAR + participle = agrees (escrita with carta).
